[MUJAHID:v1p316#2/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says Joseph asked the released prisoner to mention him to the king; the prisoner forgot until the king dreamed. Satan made Joseph forget remembrance of his Lord and direct his plea to the king, so Joseph remained imprisoned for years because he had said to mention him to the king.
[FARRA:v2p46/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The wording إني أرى is understood as a dream in Arabic; if the king meant waking observation he would state an ordinary action, and Abraham explicitly says he saw the vision in sleep. | mentions 37:102
[TAB-FULL:v13p177#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Although the verse does not explicitly say the king was asleep, Arabs understand 'I see myself doing this' as reporting a dream; seven fat cows, seven lean cows, and ears of grain are therefore a dream vision.
[TAB-FULL:v13p177#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari glosses the seven green ears as dreamt ears, others as seven other ears, the mala' as nobles and associates, and aftuni as 'interpret it for me.' | mentions 3:7
[TAB-FULL:v13p177#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says God showed the king a frightening dream, after which he gathered diviners and interpreters; they called it confused dreams and admitted they could not interpret it. | mentions 12:44
[TAB-FULL:v13p177#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Ishaq names the king as al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid and says he recognized the vision as true but did not know its interpretation. | mentions 8:48
[ZAJJAJ:v3p112/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | ʿIjāf are cows that have reached the extreme of emaciation; the malāʾ are people consulted whose opinions are followed. 
[ZAJJAJ:v3p112/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The lām in li-l-ruʾyā marks the object and clarifies ‘interpret’; ʿabara a dream means report its eventual outcome, by analogy with crossing to the far bank. 
[IBNABIHATIM:v7p2150/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | The king, Rayyan ibn al-Walid, saw a disturbing dream that he recognized as true but could not interpret, so he asked his court for an interpretation.
[IBNABIHATIM:v7p2150/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي | reports | God showed the king a troubling dream of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean cows and seven green ears eaten by dry ones; he consulted sorcerers, soothsayers, physiognomists, and bird augurs, who called it confused dreams and professed no knowledge.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p192/r7] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The word ruʾyā is read with tafkhīm or imālah; imālah signals that its final alif is feminine because it corresponds in form to tāʾ.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p192/r8] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī reportedly makes imālah in this ruʾyā but opens the word in ruʾyāka; this is mistaken if meant to distinguish case, but sound if showing both permissible dialects. | mentions 12:5
[THALABI:v5p225/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi says the seven years of this imprisonment came after five earlier years; as release approached, the Egyptian king dreamed of seven fat cows consumed by seven lean ones.
[THALABI:v5p225/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The king also saw seven green ears and seven dry ones and summoned the elite to interpret the dream.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p41/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The king who saw the dream was al-Walid ibn al-Rayan.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p41/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The dream both became the means of Joseph's release and warned of drought, allowing people to prepare.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p41/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Because the king did not know the dream's interpretation, he announced it to his people so anyone with interpretive knowledge could hear and explain it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p126/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | reports | The king saw seven fat cows swallowed by seven lean cows until none remained visible, and seven ripe green ears overcome by seven dry ears; he asked his court to interpret it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p126/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الليث | reports | عجف means loss of fat; عجاف describes thin animals with no flesh or fat.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p126/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The plural عجاف is an anomalous pattern for أعجف/عجفاء, analogized to سمان; only a small set of adjectives show this pattern.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p126/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن السكيت | reports | Ibn al-Sikkīt transmits from al-Farrāʾ variants with kasra in عجف and several comparable forms.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p126/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن دريد | reports | Ibn Durayd defines عجف as thick bones stripped of flesh.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p127/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | The meaning of أفتوني and استفتاء was discussed earlier in the commentary on al-Nisāʾ.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p127/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الأزهري | reports | The verb عَبَرَ for interpreting a dream comes from crossing to the far bank: an interpreter considers the dream's two sides and traces it from beginning to end.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p127/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أحمد بن يحيى | reports | Aḥmad b. Yaḥyā calls the lām in للرؤيا a lām of attachment and reads the sense as “if you are interpreters of the dream.”
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p127/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbārī treats the lām as emphatic; another analysis gives it the sense “toward,” directing interpretation toward the dream.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p127/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says the lām introduces the object to clarify the meaning of interpreting.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p127/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | The verb is used as an adjective meaning interpreters, as in 4:90 and 3:7; elsewhere an adjective can replace a verb, as in 7:193. | mentions 4:90, 3:7, 7:193
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:41-44/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The king dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones and seven green ears of grain alongside dry ones.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p446#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | As Yusuf's release neared, Egypt's king Rayyan ibn al-Walid saw seven fat cows eaten by seven lean cows and seven ripe green ears overcome by seven dry ears, but found no interpreter.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p446#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Making fat an adjective of cows distinguishes the seven by a type of cow, whereas making it describe seven would distinguish by genus before adding the quality.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p446#2/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The word ʿijāf cannot alone specify a count's genus; substantivized adjectives such as horsemen or companions can serve as classifiers, unlike mere adjectives.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p446#2/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The dry ears are also seven: the context's count governs cows and green ears, and the word ukhar means seven others.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p446#2/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Coordinating dry ears as a genitive adjective of the green ears would conflict with ukhar, which requires them to be other than the seven.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p446#2/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The addressed council comprises leading scholars and sages.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p446#2/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | The lam in lil-ruʾyā may explain the object, compensate when an object precedes its verb, mark competence as a predicate, or accompany an understood verb of volunteering. | mentions 12:20
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p446#2/r8] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The basic sense of interpreting a dream is to state its end or outcome, like crossing a river to reach its far side; taʾwīl likewise names its destination.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p446#2/r9] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | prefers | The light form ʿabartu is the form trusted authorities use; he says they reject the doubled form, taʿbīr, and muʿabbir.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p247#3/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The king says he sees the dream while describing a past dream, using the present because the vision is being contemplated now.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p247#3/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | A report adds that seven thin cows emerged after the fat cows from a river and ate them, then disappeared inside their bellies.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p247#3/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | ʿIjāf describes cows that have reached the extreme of emaciation.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p247#3/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | A poet’s description of Meccan men as emaciated witnesses this meaning of عجاف.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p247#3/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | Readers differ in pronouncing the two hamzas of أفتوني; another group pronounces an intervening alif as wāw.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p247#3/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The lām in للرؤيا links and emphasizes the fronted object; dream interpretation is named for crossing a river from one bank to another, as the interpreter reaches the dream’s endpoint.
[TABRISI:12:43-49#2/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Dreams may come from God or angels and admit interpretation, from Satan without interpretation, or from the sleeper's beliefs and prior thoughts.
[TABRISI:12:43-49#2/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | ʿAjaf denotes loss of fat; aʿjaf and ʿajfāʾ are the masculine and feminine forms, with ʿijāf as an unusual plural.
[TABRISI:12:43-49/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · جعفر بن محمد | reports | Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad reads سبع سنابل rather than the form used in the verse text.
[TABRISI:12:44-46/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The king was the Egyptian ruler al-Walid ibn Rayyan, and al-ʿAziz was his minister; the majority understand the vision as occurring in sleep.
[TABRISI:12:44-46/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The seven lean cows consume the fat ones until they disappear; the dry ears curl over and overcome the

[TABRISI:12:44-46/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The king addresses the elite; another view says the assembly was magicians and soothsayers.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p229/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The king is the chief king of Egypt; “I see” is in the present tense but can mean that he saw the dream.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p229/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · وهب بن منبه | reports | Wahb says that when Joseph's appointed prison term ended, Gabriel announced his release, kingship, and reunion with his father; that night the king dreamed of cows and grain.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p229/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The seven thin cows had reached the extreme of emaciation; the “council” are people consulted and followed in decisions.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p229/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says the lām in “for the dream” clarifies the object: “if you interpret dreams.”
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p229/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari gives two functions for the lām: emphasis or the sense “toward,” directing the interpretation to the dream.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p229/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Interpreting a dream means telling the outcome toward which its matter will turn; the word is derived from crossing to a riverbank.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p118#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The advisers did not deny that dream interpretation exists; they said the king's vision was an incoherent mixture beyond their skill, while implying a more accomplished interpreter might understand it.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p118/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | As Joseph's release approached, the Egyptian king dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean cows and seven green ears overgrown by seven dry ones; his advisers called it confused and un-interpretable.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p118/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الليث | reports | Al-Layth defines ʿajaf as loss of fat and notes that ʿajaf is an anomalous plural matching the opposite word simān by analogy.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p118/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Some grammarians treat the lām in للرؤيا as extra because the object precedes its verb; al-Zamakhshari instead allows الرؤيا to be a predicate of kāna, with تعبرون as another predicate or a circumstantial phrase.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p118/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأزهري | reports | Al-Azhari derives dream interpretation from crossing a river: the interpreter considers the two sides of a dream and moves from images to their meaning.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p118/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A confused dream is like a bundle of mixed plants; if its elements lack proportion or relation, it resembles a bundle of disparate things.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43#2/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali says fat cattle in a town signal prosperous years, and lean cattle harsh years; in a coastal town during sailing season they may signal arriving ships, otherwise successive turmoil resembling cattle faces.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43#2/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | In Ali's interpretation, uniformly yellow cattle can mean disease; different colors, ugly horns, or fire and smoke from their mouths can signify an army, raid, or attacking enemy.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43#2/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | A cow may also symbolize a wife, servant, crop yield, or year because it bears offspring and produces yield and vegetation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43#2/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | عجاف is parsed from either of two cited verb patterns, عَجَفَ يَعْجَفُ or عَجِفَ يَعْجَفُ.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43#2/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | أفتوني في رؤياي means tell me the ruling or interpretation of my dream; ʿibārah derives from crossing a river, as an interpreter crosses toward the dream's outcome.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43#2/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says the lām in للرؤيا clarifies the object: if you interpret, namely, the dream.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | As Joseph's release neared, Gabriel told him the king's dream would bring freedom and power; the account identifies the king as al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid and describes seven fat cows from a dry river eaten by seven lean cows and green ears consumed by dry ears.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | The king was frightened and consulted courtiers and experts in divination, astrology, soothsaying, and magic; they dismissed his vision as mixed dreams.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عطاء | reports | Ibn Jurayj reports Ata's view that confused dreams are false or mistaken visions.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الضحاك عن ابن عباس | reports | Al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, says some dreams are true and some are confused, meaning false.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الهروي | reports | Al-Harawi glosses أضغاث as mixed dreams, from the word for a bundle of plants or grass, hence a muddled vision.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says confused dreams are frightening jumble and terrors.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda defines confused dreams as visions with no interpretation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:43/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The feminine numeral سبع precedes feminine بقرات; سمان is an adjective of cows, though outside Quranic wording it could describe the numeral, like the cited construction in 67:3. | mentions 67:3
[BAYDAWI-FULL:12:43/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | As Joseph's release approached, the king dreamed of seven fat cows emerging from a dry river and seven emaciated cows swallowing them, along with green ears and dry ears; the latter overtook and overwhelmed the former.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:12:43/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The green ears had formed grain, while the dry ones had ripened; their state is omitted because the cow imagery has already explained it.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:12:43/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The feminine plural descriptors reflect how the first adjective distinguishes the cows and the second needs the noun to identify the sex; 'emaciated' is cast as the opposite of 'fat.'
[BAYDAWI-FULL:12:43/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The king asks the council to interpret the dream; ta'bir is passage from imagined forms to their corresponding psychic meanings, and the lam either marks clarification, strengthens a delayed verb, or reflects a verb that takes lam.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p190#3/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The Egyptian king al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones and seven green ears overcome by seven dry ears; the unusual vision distressed him.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p190#3/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Joseph's ordeal began with a dream and his deliverance also came through one.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p190#3/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Sīmān is a regular plural of fat; ʿijāf is a plural of lean, an unusual pattern for feminine afʿal adjectives, modeled on its opposite sīmān by pairing opposites.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p190#3/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Although only the green ears are explicitly numbered, the structure repeatedly centers on seven, so the dry ears also number seven.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p190#3/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Al-malāʾ means the realm's prominent scholars and sages.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p190#3/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The lām in li-l-ruʾyā may clarify, reinforce a fronted object that is weaker in governing the verb, or form a predicate of kāna; taʿburūn can be another predicate or a circumstantial clause.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p190#3/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | To interpret a dream is to state its outcome, like crossing a river to its far bank; taʾwīl likewise names its end or return.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p190#3/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | prefers | The light form ʿabartu is the established reading; the source says scholars reject the heavy form, taʿbīr, and muʿabbir.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p265/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Saman is the familiar noun and verbal noun from samina; samīn is its active participle, an irregular pairing of forms.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p265/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Al-ʿajfāʾ describes an extremely emaciated female animal.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p279/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The Egyptian king, named al-Rayyān ibn al-Walīd, sees seven fat cows from a dry river swallowed by seven lean cows, and seven ripe green ears overpowered by seven dry ones.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The present-tense أرى recounts a scene as if occurring now; أفتوني في رؤياي shows it is a dream.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abū Jaʿfar assimilates the hamza in ruʾyā through an unusual sequence of sound changes; grammarians call it irregular because the waw substitution is optional.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The lām in للرؤيا strengthens the verb's access to its object when the object precedes; it does not work as well when the object follows.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | The apparent syntax makes تعبرون the predicate of كنتم.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī offers three more complex parses: الرؤيا as an explanatory topic with an omitted object, as predicate of كان with another predicate or circumstantial phrase, or as governed by an understood verb meaning undertake interpretation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Dream interpretation is called عبور by analogy with crossing a river, as the interpreter reaches the vision's final meaning.

2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Samān modifies the cows rather than the numeral, distinguishing a kind of cow; modifying the number itself would wrongly imply that the seven were fat.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The distinction between ثلاث رجال كرام and ثلاثة رجال كرام shows that describing the counted subset differs from describing the people as a whole.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Seven is not annexed to the adjective ajāf because numerals normally annex to adjectives only in poetry; exceptions are adjectives used as nouns, such as knights or companions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The mention of seven cows implies that the lean cows are also seven cows, with the counted noun omitted before their adjective.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The plural ajāf follows the opposite adjective samān, though the expected plural of ajfāʾ is ʿujuf, like khudr for khadrāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The division between fat and lean cows implies seven ears in each division; the numeral is omitted before أخر يابسات.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p280/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Al-malaʾ are the king's leading officials who attend him.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p281/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | A poem cited by al-Mubarrad illustrates the use of the ungeminated verb ʿabara for interpreting a dream.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:43#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Number words are not normally annexed to adjectives; adjectives follow the number as nominative, with genitive attachment only in poetic necessity.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:43#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Three huge ones is avoided because the described noun is unknown; here cows are known, but ordinary word order still makes direct annexation unnecessary.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:43#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | عجاف is the plural of عجفاء; the expected plural عجف is analogically leveled to سمان because the terms are opposites.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:43#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari defines عجف as extreme emaciation and cites the line about Meccans in years of famine.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:43#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib relates عجف to a thin blade, aversion from food or a person, and encountering thin livestock.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:43#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | وأخر coordinates with سبع, not سنبلات; the omitted number is seven, understood from the matching groups of cows and ears.
[SAMIN-DURR:12:43#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari infers that the dry ears are also seven because the passage repeatedly focuses on groups of seven.
